subject: paediatrics
title: Neonatal Jaundice, Kramer Staging and Kernicterus

steps.tx: Yellowish discolouration of the skin and sclera resulting from bilirubin accumulation is **neonatal hyperbilirubinemia**, visible when serum levels exceed five milligrams per deciliter. Neonates possess higher circulating red cell mass with a shortened lifespan of eighty days, combined with immature hepatic uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase enzyme activity and enhanced enterohepatic reabsorption.
steps.say: Neonatal jaundice becomes visible at five milligrams per deciliter due to high red cell turnover and immature clearance.

vis.alt: Clinical assessment of neonatal jaundice showing Kramer dermal zones and phototherapy.
vis.caption: Kramer dermal icterus zones and phototherapy isomerization mechanism. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Clinical differentiation requires separating benign physiological jaundice from pathological hyperbilirubinemia. Classic **physiological neonatal jaundice** appears after twenty-four hours of life, peaks on day three to four at twelve to fifteen milligrams per deciliter in term infants, and completely resolves by ten to fourteen days. The infant remains clinically active, feeds vigorously, and passes normal yellow stools.
steps.say: Physiological jaundice appears after twenty-four hours, peaks on day four, and clears by two weeks.

rows: Exceeds 15 to 17 mg/dL in term infants
Persists beyond 14 days in term (21 days preterm)

steps.tx: Bedside non-invasive visual evaluation relies on **Kramer dermal icterus zones**, assessing cephalocaudal progression under natural daylight. Jaundice advances in an orderly fashion: Zone one covers head and neck (approx 5 mg/dL), Zone two reaches the umbilicus (approx 8 mg/dL), Zone three reaches the knees (approx 12 mg/dL), and Zone five involves the palms and soles (>15 mg/dL).
steps.say: Kramer zones track cephalocaudal jaundice progression from five on the face to over fifteen on palms.

rows: Upper trunk down to the umbilicus
Lower abdomen and thighs down to knees
Arms and lower legs below knees
Palms of hands and soles of feet

steps.tx: Assessing the risk of progressive hyperbilirubinemia utilizes the **Bhutani hour specific nomogram**. By plotting total serum bilirubin against exact postnatal age in hours, the nomogram stratifies infants into low, intermediate, and high-risk zones. Values plotted above the ninety-fifth percentile designate high risk, requiring immediate diagnostic laboratory evaluation, intensified monitoring, and phototherapy.
steps.say: The Bhutani nomogram plots hour-specific bilirubin to identify neonates at risk of severe hyperbilirubinemia.

right.title: Clinical Applications
points: Guides safe discharge timing from nursery
Determines follow-up schedule within 24 to 48 hours

steps.tx: Unconjugated hydrophobic bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier when binding capacity is saturated, producing **acute bilirubin encephalopathy**. Phase one manifests with lethargy, poor feeding, and generalized hypotonia. Phase two is characterized by irritability, high-pitched crying, retrocollis, and opisthotonos. Phase three features stupor, apnea, seizures, and death from cardiorespiratory arrest.
steps.say: Acute bilirubin encephalopathy progresses from lethargy to hypertonia, retrocollis, and seizures.

rows: Lethargy, poor suck, loss of Moro, hypotonia
Fully reversible with immediate exchange transfusion
Partially reversible, high risk of permanent injury

steps.tx: Chronic irreversible neurological sequelae from bilirubin deposition in the basal ganglia is **chronic kernicterus**. Autopsy demonstrates intense yellow staining and neuronal necrosis within the globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, and auditory brainstem nuclei. Survivors exhibit choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, sensorineural hearing loss, dental enamel hypoplasia, and upward gaze palsy.
steps.say: Chronic kernicterus features choreoathetosis, sensorineural hearing loss, and upward gaze palsy.

left.title: Anatomical Target Nuclei
points: Oculomotor cranial nerve nuclei in brainstem

steps.tx: The primary therapeutic intervention for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia is **narrow spectrum phototherapy**. Blue-green light with wavelengths between 460 and 490 nanometers penetrates skin capillaries, transforming toxic unconjugated 4Z,15Z-bilirubin into configurational and structural photoisomers. The major structural photoisomer is lumirubin, an irreversible water-soluble product excreted rapidly in bile and urine without requiring hepatic glucuronidation.
steps.say: Phototherapy converts bilirubin into water-soluble lumirubin, which is excreted without hepatic conjugation.

rows: Rapidly excreted in bile and urine without conjugation
Excreted in bile, can revert to unconjugated bilirubin
Excreted slowly in urine, minor clinical pathway

steps.tx: When serum bilirubin reaches critical neurotoxic thresholds or fails to respond to intensive phototherapy, **double volume exchange transfusion** is performed. Removing twice the infant's circulating blood volume replaces eighty-five percent of circulating erythrocytes and lowers serum bilirubin by half. Performed via an umbilical venous catheter, it removes antibody-coated red blood cells and maternal antibodies in hemolytic disease.
steps.say: Double volume exchange transfusion replaces eighty-five percent of red cells and removes toxic bilirubin rapidly.

left.title: Procedural Technique
points: Aliquots of 5 to 10 mL/kg pushed and pulled
Infuse 1 mL calcium gluconate per 100 mL blood

right.title: Therapeutic Objectives
points: Corrects severe anemia and heart failure
